environmentalPersistence: Very high — does not degrade; accumulates in soil

morphologicalEffects.heightSuppression: Moderate — osmotic stress reduces growth; at low levels Mg²⁺ is actually beneficial
morphologicalEffects.leafSize: Mildly to moderately reduced at high doses
morphologicalEffects.leafCurl: Moderate — similar mechanism to NaCl but less severe (Mg²⁺ is a plant nutrient)
morphologicalEffects.wilting: Moderate to strong — osmotic component dominant at high concentration
morphologicalEffects.chlorosis: Moderate — Cl⁻ ion toxicity; paradoxically Mg deficiency can cause chlorosis (Mg is the central chlorophyll atom) but excess MgCl₂ delivers too much Cl⁻
morphologicalEffects.necrosis: Moderate — Cl⁻ toxicity causes tip burn
morphologicalEffects.newVsOldLeaves: Old leaves show Cl⁻ burn first; younger leaves show osmotic wilting first

physiologyEffects.waterUptake: Impaired at high concentrations — osmotic effect
physiologyEffects.nutrientTransport: Mildly disrupted — Mg²⁺ competes with Ca²⁺ and K⁺ at high concentrations

molecularEffects.oxidativeStress: Moderate — osmotic and Cl⁻ ion stress

microbiomeEffects.diversityReduction: Moderate — less severe than NaCl due to Mg²⁺ being a micronutrient

visualSimulation.colorChanges: Green → wilting/curling → mild yellowing → tip burn
visualSimulation.damagePattern: Similar to NaCl but less severe; tip burn lighter
visualSimulation.heatmapGlow: Moderate — proline and betaine osmolyte signature
visualSimulation.recoveryVisual: Good — better recovery than NaCl; Mg²⁺ is a nutrient and soil can buffer

synergies.synergyNote: MgCl₂ is a common component of road salt mixtures (with NaCl and CaCl₂) — combined salt stress is the real-world scenario for roadside vegetation
synergies.antagonismNote: High Mg²⁺ can antagonize Ca²⁺ and K⁺ uptake; but at sub-toxic levels Mg²⁺ is beneficial for chlorophyll

educationalContext.realWorldSources: Road deicing salt (second most common after NaCl); industrial salt brines; natural saline soils; seawater
educationalContext.agriculturalUse: Not intentionally applied as stressor; small amounts used as Mg fertilizer
educationalContext.humanToxicity: Very low — used as a food additive (tofu coagulant); supplement in sports drinks
educationalContext.climateLink: Increased road salt use in northern cities combined with more variable winters (less snow but more freezing rain) affects urban street trees and roadside vegetation
educationalContext.indoorOutdoor: Primarily outdoor — road runoff and saline soil
educationalContext.whyStudentsCare: Road salt is the reason trees along city sidewalks die young — the brown-tipped Norway maples lining urban streets are showing MgCl₂ and NaCl stress. Students can observe it in their own neighborhoods.
educationalContext.realWorldIssue: Road salt runoff, urban tree health, groundwater salinization, winter road management

sources: Munns R, Tester M (2008). Mechanisms of salinity tolerance. Annual Review of Plant Biology, 59, 651–681.
Blomqvist G, Johansson E (1999). Airborne spreading and deposition of de-icing salt. Science of the Total Environment, 235(1–3), 161–168.
Cekstere G, Nikodemus O, Osvalde A (2008). Toxic impact of the de-icing material to street greenery in Riga, Latvia. Urban Forestry & Urban Greening, 7(3), 207–217.
